title: The missing thirteenth site
headline: Thirteen sites fit. A walk still tops out at twelve.
summary: Grow a disk on the triangular lattice. At squared radius 3 it can first hold 13 sites. A 13-step walk through those sites would have to close. The six tips force a cycle that leaves the center out.
scope: Two independent exact searches over all disk centers find the missing tenth point record. The ninth positive walk record is 14, refuting the proposed equality. Kittipassorn, Phetmak and Sriamorn independently tabulated the point count.

frames.label: Sites
frames.caption: At squared radius 3, there are six tips, six inner neighbors and one center.

frames.label: Forced edges
frames.caption: Every tip needs both its edges. The resulting twelve-edge loop leaves the center out.

title: A one-ångström discrepancy in the hydrogen sequence
headline: At level 15, the recurrence misses by one ångström.
summary: The source’s rounding rule gives 205,035 Å. Barker’s recurrence predicts 205,034 Å. The discrepancy follows from just two tabulated levels, even if the Rydberg constant varies within their rounding bounds.
scope: Two independent checks: a Lean certificate for the published program and a rational interval calculation for the tabulated values.

title: A one-ångström discrepancy in the wavelength gaps
headline: The gap first misses by one ångström at level 14.
summary: The jump from level 14 to level 15 is 26,427 Å. The proposed recurrence for adjacent gaps gives 26,426 Å. Both hydrogen entries measure the same discrepancy.
scope: Lean checks the proposed rule at every earlier index in its stated range and verifies the first failure.

title: A shifted toppling count on the sandpile ring
headline: The one-row sandpile count is shifted by one.
summary: A two-site ring has one active pile. It fires once and then stops. The printed formula gives two. For a ring of length n ≥ 2, the correct count is A023855(n − 1).
scope: The Omega Institute previously proved the corrected formula. Our standalone Lean proof refutes the printed indexing. A separate simulation checks 150 legal firing orders across 50 sizes.

frames.label: Before
frames.caption: On the two-site ring the active site starts with four grains. The other site is a sink.

frames.label: After one firing
frames.caption: Two grains reach the sink. The two vertical self-loops return their grains, leaving the active site stable.

title: A theta series for the CHSH winning probability
headline: A theta series sums to the CHSH winning probability.
summary: Split a Gaussian lattice sum into even and odd indices. The theta transformation fixes their ratio, giving the exact value of the proposed series.
scope: Lean 4.33.1 checks the complete series identity, including absolute convergence. The statement is in upstream review. Somos recorded the equivalent theta quotient in 2022.

frames.label: Even pairs
frames.caption: The transformed lattice sum splits into equal-parity pairs. Even–even pairs contribute A².

frames.label: Odd pairs
frames.caption: Odd–odd pairs contribute B², where B = (√2 − 1)A.

frames.label: Quotient
frames.caption: Combining the two sums gives A²/(A²+B²), the CHSH winning probability.

title: Six photons and three target colors
headline: Can six photons share three perfectly matched colors?
summary: In this pair-source model, the answer is no. Every higher-dimensional solution would restrict to three colors. Lean checks the complete six-photon theorem, including sources with arbitrary complex edge weights.
scope: Lean checks the six-vertex theorem with arbitrary complex weights. The physics restriction was known; the rigidity proof is an attributed port of Rishi Rajasekaran’s work.

links.label: Editorial draft on Left to Solve

frames.label: Pairing I
frames.caption: A perfect matching pairs each of the six output vertices exactly once.

frames.label: Pairing II
frames.caption: Another way to pair the same outputs. There are fifteen possible pairings before amplitudes are assigned.

frames.label: Dimension
frames.caption: With three colors the matching equations are inconsistent. Restricting to three colors also rules out every higher dimension in this model.

title: When a periodic wave’s spectral trace can turn
headline: Can a spectral band turn around inside its allowed range?
summary: With a real periodic potential the slope cannot vanish there. An imaginary cosine potential can produce a stationary point inside the band. The answer depends on an assumption left unstated in the question.
scope: The catalogue leaves the potential’s range unstated. Lean checks the real matrix inequality; the full argument treats both cases.

frames.label: Real potential
frames.caption: For real, continuous, symmetric periodic potentials and real shear, the trace has no stationary point when |f(z)| < 1.

frames.label: Complex potential
frames.caption: An imaginary cosine potential gives a stationary point with |f(z)| < 1. The distinction concerns the potential, not just the energy.

title: Why every record walk closes
headline: Every optimal record walk longer than one step closes.
summary: At the smallest radius that fits a record-length walk, closing the loop is the only way to attain that length. A theorem of Reay and Zamfirescu covers large disks except for one 13-site star. A smaller explicit 12-cycle handles that exception.
scope: Written proof for every record length. Lean checks the finite geometric witnesses. The general argument invokes the published Hamiltonian-cycle theorem.

frames.label: Exception
frames.caption: The six tips of this 13-site disk force a cycle around the center.

frames.label: Smaller disk
frames.caption: A 12-edge cycle already fits at squared radius 7/3. It supplies paths of every length through twelve.

title: Full disks and longest walks at integer diameters
headline: At every integer diameter from two up, a cycle can visit every site in a fullest disk.
summary: The maximum number of steps equals the maximum number of sites among all disk placements. The only exceptional graph is too wide for diameters two and three. From diameter four onward, a competing disk already holds 19 sites.
scope: This proves the proposed equality for both integer sequences using the same published graph theorem as the record-walk result.

frames.label: Diameters 2–3
frames.caption: Opposite tips of the only exceptional graph are too far apart for either integer diameter.

frames.label: Diameter 4
frames.caption: At diameter 4 a site-centered disk contains 19 sites. Any larger integer diameter retains this witness.

title: Boundary-covering loops on a five-row strip
headline: Twenty states count loops on a strip of any length.
summary: Draw a single loop on a grid five vertices wide. It must visit every vertex along the boundary. A cut across the grid sees only twenty ways to connect the loose ends. One vector identity then proves Manyama’s proposed recurrence for every length from eleven onward.
scope: Exact integer proof with an independent small-grid enumeration. Width five is fixed.

frames.label: 2 columns
frames.caption: The unique boundary-covering cycle on two columns.

frames.label: 3 columns
frames.caption: Five cycles cover the boundary. The perimeter is one of them.

frames.label: 4 columns
frames.caption: There are 36 cycles on four columns. The example shown follows the perimeter.

title: Corner-to-corner paths through the middle
headline: Five states count self-avoiding paths through the center.
summary: Walk between opposite corners of a three-row grid and pass through the middle vertex. Adding one column on either side of the center acts on a space of dimension 25. That makes 25 exact zero checks enough to prove the recurrence for every length in Manyama’s conjecture.
scope: Exact transfer proof for the stated fixed-width strip.

frames.label: 3 columns
frames.caption: Ten paths qualify. Here the path reaches the center on its second step.

title: Self-avoiding crossings of a four-column strip
headline: Twelve states settle the four-column recurrence.
summary: Start at the northwest corner and finish at the southwest corner without revisiting a site. A cut between rows retains twelve possible connection patterns. They yield the order-twelve recurrence and generating function proposed by Colin Barker for Gottfried’s sequence.
scope: Exact transfer proof for the stated fixed-width strip.

frames.label: 1 row
frames.caption: Both corners coincide. The empty path counts once.

frames.label: 2 rows
frames.caption: Four paths qualify. This one crosses at the far right.

frames.label: 3 rows
frames.caption: There are 28 paths between the two left corners. One example is highlighted.

title: Counting prudent walks ending at a corner
headline: An exact count for walks that refuse to step toward their own trail.
summary: For two-sided prudent walks that end at the northeast corner of their bounding box, Mathar proposed a nine-term-lag relation. Its full verification reduces to a polynomial remainder of exactly zero. It holds at every length from nine onward.
scope: The proof uses Mireille Bousquet-Mélou’s published generating function. The replay uses SymPy 1.14.0.

frames.label: Straight east
frames.caption: Four eastward steps never point toward a visited site. The endpoint is the northeast corner.

frames.label: Turn south
frames.caption: East, south, east, north. Each successive endpoint stays on the top or right of its current box.

frames.label: Turn west
frames.caption: North, west, north, east. This is another of the 24 qualifying four-step walks.
